**Abstract**

Electrocardiography (ECG) is one of the most widely used tools in medicine, although it is not used to its full potential. This is because standard diagnosis and analysis reduce rich waveform data to simple averages, discarding beat-to-beat variability that reflects aging, autonomic function, and disease risk. While deep learning and AI approaches often leverage the full ECG signal, they often lack clinical interpretability, feature transparency, and cross-cohort generalizability.

Here, we present PyHEARTS, an algorithmic framework for scalable and interpretable ECG analysis. PyHEARTS enables what we call “beat-level phenotyping”, capturing a detailed physiological fingerprint from each heartbeat with full transparency and precision. The toolbox extracts 139 features per beat using Gaussian fitting and morphological modeling. It captures standard ECG intervals along with novel morphological and variability features, including waveform sharpness, rise and decay asymmetry, deflection onset and offset timing, amplitude ratios, and voltage integrals, among others.

With 2.9 million beats from more than 30,000 individuals from four datasets, PyHEARTS achieves high reconstruction fidelity (R2 \> 0.9 in 76% of cycles), strong test-retest reliability (median ICC above 0.95), and stable performance across datasets, sessions, and species. In predicting biological age, PyHEARTS achieves age-prediction performance within the range reported for deep learning–based ECG age models (R2 of 0.44 and MAE of 9.1 years), despite using only linear models and interpretable features.

Beat-to-beat variability emerged as the most powerful predictor of biological age. Morphological features related to QRS shape and repolarization added additional physiological insight. PyHEARTS also generalizes to mouse ECG with sub-millisecond precision, enabling direct comparison between human and animal cardiac dynamics critical for linking animal model research to human clinical applications.

By preserving physiological detail at scale, PyHEARTS turns ECG from a static diagnostic snapshot into a dynamic, high-resolution signal for precision phenotyping, aging research, and interpretable modeling of cardiovascular physiology in humans and animals.

**Introduction**

Electrocardiography (ECG) is a widely used, cost-effective tool in both clinical practice and physiological research. It provides a non-invasive, real-time view of the heart’s electrical activity and overall function. ECG-derived features, particularly heart rate (HR) and heart rate variability (HRV), are established biomarkers of aging, autonomic regulation, stress, and disease[1–6](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Et5qPq). These metrics are routinely applied across clinical and research contexts. Beyond traditional cardiac applications, ECG measures have also been linked to cognitive performance, psychiatric disorders, epilepsy, and other systemic conditions[7–13](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?wxBejX). This breadth highlights the growing importance of ECG as a diagnostic and translational tool.

ECG features include deflections, durations, and morphology, with peaks serving as reference landmarks for clinically relevant intervalsEach deflection in the ECG waveform (P, Q, R, S, and T peaks) reflects a specific physiological event in cardiac electrophysiology[14](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?XWSzvK). Yet standard statistical aggregation methods often obscure rapid, transient shifts that reflect moment-to-moment autonomic regulation and cardiovascular adaptation. To improve signal quality, researchers typically average ECG waveforms across beats[15](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?82Ggto). This simplifies interpretation and supports large-scale analyses using summary statistics. However, it also removes beat-to-beat variability, potentially discarding information related to age, sex, health status, or individual traits, and can further remove information in the morphology of individual beats. Clinical workflows face analogous limitations. Many clinicians still rely on manual ECG inspection, often of representative single heartbeats, using calipers or equivalent software approaches to assess waveform features[16](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?cwpS8A). These approaches form the foundation of modern ECG analysis and remain the standard for clinical interval measurement; however, their outputs are typically limited to discrete landmarks rather than continuous, beat-resolved representations of waveform morphology. These tools are practical, but lack the resolution needed to capture dynamic, fine-grained but small-scale waveform changes that may carry clinical or biological relevance.

To address these limitations, a substantial body of work has focused on automated ECG delineation using classical signal processing approaches[17–19](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?aibAch). These include derivative- and threshold-based methods, wavelet and discrete wavelet transform (DWT) techniques, and template-matching strategies designed to identify fiducial points such as P-wave onset, QRS complexes, and T-wave offset with high temporal precision[20–22](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?3Ozk0O). Several open-source toolboxes implementing these approaches are widely used in both research and clinical settings[23,24](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?NDHKy0). While these methods provide accurate and efficient delineation of key ECG landmarks, they primarily focus on discrete fiducial timing and amplitudes and typically do not preserve continuous beat-to-beat morphological variability or provide a generative representation of waveform shape across long recordings.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for ECG analysis have enabled end-to-end modeling approaches, including automated classification of cardiac conditions, estimation of biological or “ECG age,” and stratification of cardiovascular risk directly from raw waveforms[25–29](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?qVsnUU). These methods often achieve high predictive accuracy and can outperform traditional ECG-derived metrics. In parallel, recent work has introduced explainable AI techniques for ECG analysis, using attention mechanisms, saliency maps, and hybrid architectures to provide post-hoc insight into model decision-making[30–34](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?23355r). However, these explanations remain largely model-centric, identifying signal regions that influence predictions rather than yielding physiologically grounded parameters that directly characterize beat-level cardiac dynamics. As a result, clinicians may be unable to explain why a specific prediction was made or assess whether a model will generalize across populations, devices, or species. This creates a divide between low-resolution manual tools that discard beat-level variability and high-capacity learning-based models that provide limited access to underlying physiological structure.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have enabled end-to-end analysis of ECG signals, including automated classification of cardiac conditions, estimation of biological or “ECG age,” and stratification of cardiovascular risk directly from raw waveformsautomat, age prediction and risk stratification using ECG waveforms[35,36](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?jIgZ0h). These approaches often achieve high predictive accuracy and can outperform traditional ECG-derived metricsmodels can diagnose cardiac conditions directly from raw signals and often outperform traditional metrics in accuracy[37,38](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?aCu42x). In parallel, the field has begun to adopt explainable AI techniques that provide post-hoc insights into model decision-making. However, these explanations remain largely model-centric, describing which signal regions or features influence predictions, rather than yielding physiologically grounded parameters that directly characterize cardiac dynamics.Deep learning models have also been used to infer demographic and physiological traits such as biological or “ECG age” from surface recordings, with deviations from chronological age linked to cardiovascular risk[39](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?2oMgaZ). Despite their success, they present a major limitation. Most are black-box systems that offer little insight into how predictions are made. Physicians often cannot explain why a model produced a specific result or whether it will generalize across populations, devices, or species. This creates a divide between low-resolution manual tools that discard variability and high-capacity models that conceal it.

Building on these prior signal-processing approaches and recent advances in machine learning,There is a growing need for we present an ECG analysis tools that can capture fine-grained physiological detail without sacrificing interpretability or flexibility. WTo address this, we drew inspiration from methods in neurophysiology, in particular the *bycycle* Python package[40](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Ot62dT), which quantifies cycle-by-cycle variability in electroencephalography (EEG) signals. Neural oscillations have nonsinusoidal waveforms that are often distorted or lost through averaging or spectral decomposition methods that assume sinusoidal structure. Parameterizing individual waveform features has revealed underlying physiological mechanisms, improved understanding of diseases such as Parkinson’s, and contributed key features to ML models for mood prediction[41,42](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?tw2zlO). Building on this approach, we developed PyHEARTS (Python Heart Evaluation and Analysis for Rhythm and Temporal Shape), a framework for extracting beat-by-beat ECG features that captures detailed cardiac variability in an interpretable and reproducible format. Unlike prior beat-level approaches that focus on fiducial timing alone, PyHEARTS provides a generative, interpretable parameterization of waveform morphology that preserves beat-to-beat structure. This represents a shift in signal analysis from summary metrics toward preserving the full temporal and morphological structure of the signal.

PyHEARTS directly addresses the limitations of current ECG methods by enabling high-resolution feature extraction across varied datasets and recording setups. The toolbox captures 139 features per beat, including standard ECG metrics such as RR intervals, QT duration, and HRV, along with novel features that are rarely quantified, including rise and decay times and waveform sharpness (**Supplementary Table 1**). Using four datasets and an analytic sample of 30,686 participants and over 2.9 million beats (see **Table 1** for dataset summaries), we show that PyHEARTS offers high test-retest reliability and strong overall accuracy. PyHEARTS is also capable of reconstructing full ECG time series from beat-level features, paving the way for future applications in ECG digital-twinning. PyHEARTS also generalizes across species by accurately parameterizing the mouse ECG, a key step for translational research. Finally, we demonstrate its utility in age classification. Age prediction is used here as a representative downstream task to assess the informativeness, stability, and physiological relevance of the extracted features, rather than as an attempt to optimize predictive accuracy or compete with end-to-end deep learning models. PyHEARTS achieves performance within the range reported for deep learning–based ECG age models, while preserving interpretability and beat-level physiological structure. matching the performance of much more complex, black box AI/ML models, while preserving interpretability. By retaining beat-level variability, PyHEARTS enables more precise and transparent analysis of cardiac dynamics and individual physiology.

Although beat-by-beat ECG analysis has been explored previously, most existing approaches focus on extracting fiducial timing or summary statistics per beat. PyHEARTS advances this paradigm by providing a generative, physiologically grounded parameterization of waveform morphology that preserves continuous beat-to-beat structure.

**Results**

We analyzed cardiac cycles across four datasets to assess ECG reconstruction fidelity and waveform feature consistency: Autonomic Aging (AA)[43](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?iUCihW), Physikalisch Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB-XL)[44](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?tFqxBp), Shandong Provincial Hospital (SPH)[45](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?B9TxM0), and Massachusetts General Hospital/Marquette Foundation (MGH)[46](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?03Upkf). An overview of the full processing pipeline is shown in Figure 1\. 

After data cleaning, our final analytical sample size was 31,885 individuals and 2.9 million beats. The breakdown for specific datasets is as follows: AA (n \= 1,1107), MGH (n \= 228), PTB-XL (n \= 4,967), and SPH (n \= 25,583). Our analyses revealed substantial differences in morphology, reconstruction accuracy, and subject-level quality across datasets. As shown in Figure 2, key measures such as waveform shape, R2 fidelity, and reconstruction error varied systematically, with consistent performance hierarchies emerging between cohorts.

**Dataset-level Feature Differences**

We first compared ECG morphology across datasets. For visualization, we present four cross-peak exemplary features: P-wave rise time, Q-wave sharpness, R-wave rise–decay ratio, and T-wave duration (**Fig. 2A**). All showed significant between-group differences (Kruskal–Wallis *p* \< 0.001), but effect sizes varied. P-rise, Q-sharpness, and T-duration showed small to moderate effects (η2 \= 0.013–0.032), indicating consistent morphological variability across datasets. In contrast, the R-wave rise–decay ratio had a negligible effect (η2 \= 0.0006), driven by outliers in the MGH cohort. These findings suggest that while morphology is dataset-sensitive, certain features are more robust to recording site and setup than others.

Pairwise comparisons confirmed significant dataset-level differences in morphology. For P-wave rise time, subjects in AA showed slower rise times compared to SPH and PTB-XL (Δmedian: –12 to –15 ms; Cliff’s δ \= –0.47 to –0.55), while MGH values were intermediate. Q-wave sharpness increased across cohorts in the order AA \< PTB-XL \< SPH \< MGH, with MGH displaying sharper Q-waves than all others (Δmedian vs. AA: \+66 a.u.; δ \= 0.47). T-wave duration showed the opposite trend, decreasing across the same sequence (AA \> PTB-XL \> SPH \> MGH), with differences exceeding 40 ms between AA and MGH (Cliff’s δ \= 0.31 to 0.56). In contrast, R-wave symmetry was consistent across AA, SPH, and PTB-XL, though all three showed higher symmetry than MGH (Δmedian ≈ 0.004; δ ≈ 0.17–0.18). These findings demonstrate that waveform morphology varies across datasets in consistent patterns, with AA and MGH frequently representing opposite extremes. Q-wave sharpness and T-wave duration show strong discriminability, while R-wave symmetry remains comparatively stable.

**Reconstruction Fidelity** 

Reconstruction fidelity varied across datasets (Kruskal–Wallis *H* \= 124.5, *p* \< 0.001). Of the 2.9 million cardiac cycles analyzed, 76% exceeded the high-fidelity threshold (R2 \> 0.9), with rates highest in SPH (85.6%, n \= 22,059) and PTB-XL (81.2%, n \=4,101), followed by AA (78.6%, n \=873) and MGH (70.9%, n \= 177\) (**Fig. 2B**). Pairwise comparisons showed small to moderate effect sizes between most groups (e.g., SPH vs. MGH: Cohen’s *h* \= 0.36). These findings confirm that SPH and PTB-XL achieved the highest fidelity, while reconstruction underperformed for the MGH dataset.

**Subject-Level Accuracy and Variability**

Subject-level mean R2 also differed across datasets (Kruskal–Wallis *H* \= 124.5, *p* \< 0.001; **Fig. 2C**). Median values were highest in AA (0.972, 95% CI: \[0.969, 0.974\]), followed by PTB-XL (0.962 \[0.961, 0.963\]), SPH (0.961 \[0.960, 0.962\]), and MGH (0.924 \[0.921, 0.928\]). Although AA ranked highest in accuracy, its reconstructions were less stable than those in PTB-XL or SPH. Within-subject variability, measured as the standard deviation of R2 across beats, differed (Kruskal–Wallis *H* \= 257.7, *p* \< 0.001; **Fig. 2D**). Median variability was lowest in PTB-XL (0.014), intermediate in SPH (0.018) and AA (0.020), and highest in MGH (0.037). Cliff’s δ comparisons confirmed greater variability in MGH relative to all other datasets (|δ| \= 0.40–0.47). These results highlight a tradeoff: AA achieved the highest accuracy, while PTB-XL produced the most consistent reconstructions. Reconstructions again underperformed on fronts for the MGH data.

**Reconstruction Error**

Reconstruction error, assessed via root mean square error (RMSE), also varied across datasets (Kruskal–Wallis *H* \= 308.1, *p* \< 0.001; **Fig. 2E**). Median RMSE was lowest in SPH (0.022 mV, 95% CI: \[0.021, 0.023\]) and PTB-XL (0.024 mV \[0.023, 0.025\]), higher in AA (0.025 mV \[0.024, 0.027\]), and highest in MGH (0.036 mV \[0.034, 0.038\]). Differences between SPH, PTB-XL, and AA were modest (Cliff’s δ ≤ 0.16), but comparisons with MGH showed moderate to large effects (δ \= 0.34–0.42). A similar pattern was observed for 95th percentile RMSE (Kruskal–Wallis *H* \= 134.6, *p* \< 0.001; **Fig. 2F**). PTB-XL and SPH both had median values around 0.034–0.036 mV, while MGH reached 0.057 mV. These results indicate that MGH reconstructions had both higher typical and extreme errors, suggesting reduced reliability under challenging waveform conditions.

**Correlation and Quadrant Analysis**

Reconstruction accuracy and error were inversely correlated at the subject level (Spearman ρ \= –0.61, p \< 0.001; **Fig. 2G**), indicating that higher R2 was associated with lower RMSE. This relationship held within each dataset, though the strength varied: PTB-XL (r \= –0.67), SPH (–0.60), AA (–0.50), and MGH (–0.28); all correlations were significant (p \< 0.001). To assess how these metrics jointly defined subject-level quality, we applied two predefined thresholds: mean R2 ≥ 0.9 and 95th percentile RMSE ≤ 0.1 mV. Subjects meeting both criteria were classified as high-fidelity. Most subjects in SPH (85%) and PTB-XL (79%) passed both thresholds, compared to 73% in AA and only 51% in MGH. The differences were statistically significant (χ2 \= 231.4, df \= 3, p \< 0.001; Cramér’s V \= 0.21), reflecting meaningful variation in reconstruction quality across datasets. These findings reinforce that SPH and PTB-XL consistently achieved high-fidelity reconstructions, while MGH subjects were far more likely to fall below acceptable accuracy and error thresholds.

**Post-hoc Waveform Error Analysis**

Post-hoc waveform analysis confirmed that reconstructed ECG morphology was preserved, with only minor and localized deviations (**Fig. 2H**). Across datasets, the distribution of mean absolute error (MAE) was centered below 0.1 mV (**Fig. 2I**). The percentage of cycles with MAE ≥ 0.2 mV (defined as reconstruction failures)[47–49](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?aPrCGQ) was low overall but varied by dataset (χ2 \= 10,932.3, df \= 3, p \< 0.001; Cramér’s V \= 0.165). Failure rates were highest in AA (2.04%, 10,725/526,367), followed by PTB-XL (0.87%, 429/49,301), SPH (0.33%, 29/8,739), and MGH (0.28%, 2,403/863,860) (**Fig. 2J**). Despite MGH’s lower overall fidelity, it exhibited the fewest failures, likely due to fewer cycles and tighter error clustering in its successful reconstructions. In contrast, AA had an elevated rate of outliers, despite relatively high R2 values. These results indicate that while reconstruction failures were rare overall, their distribution was not uniform. SPH and PTB-XL delivered both high accuracy and minimal outlier risk, while AA showed slightly more reconstruction instability. MGH had a lower failure rate but remained the weakest performer in terms of accuracy and consistency.

To further quantify parameterization quality, we required at least one major peak (P–T, inclusive) to be fit. Under this criterion, the proportion of beats was 87% in AA, 94% in MGH, 99.5% in PTB-XL, and 99.6% in SPH. Pairwise comparisons showed substantial absolute differences between AA and the other datasets (Δ \= 6.8–12.8%) and between MGH and PTB-XL/SPH (Δ ≈ 6.0%). By contrast, the difference between PTB-XL and SPH was 0.13% (95% CI: –0.22%, –0.05%), reflecting a negligible effect despite statistical significance due to large sample sizes.

**Temporal Validation: Between-Session** 

To evaluate temporal reproducibility, we analyzed within-subject ECG features across repeated recording sessions. Stable features such as RP amplitude difference (R\_minus\_P\_voltage\_diff\_signed) and R height showed minimal change between sessions, with median differences of 0.006 mV (95% CI: –0.001 to 0.014) and 0.001 mV (95% CI: –0.007 to 0.010), respectively (**Fig. 3A**). In contrast, less stable features such as P sharpness and Q right voltage had broader variability, with median differences of –0.393 (95% CI: –3.028 to 2.242) and –0.002 mV (95% CI: –0.004 to 0.000), respectively. Although these features were relatively less stable compared with high-amplitude metrics, their absolute variability remained small (median change \< 0.4 a.u. for P sharpness and \< 0.01 mV for Q right voltage), indicating that all features were highly repeatable overall across sessions.

Wilcoxon signed-rank tests indicated that none of the four features showed significant differences between sessions after false discovery rate (FDR) correction (all adjusted p \> 0.19). The distributions of session-wise differences reinforced these trends (**Fig. 3B**). Stable features produced narrow, symmetric histograms centered near zero, while less stable features showed wider and more asymmetric spreads. These results demonstrate that core morphological features are reproducible across sessions, and while a small subset exhibits variability, none show consistent directional change.

**Cross-Dataset ICC Agreement and Feature Reliability**

To assess the reproducibility of ECG features across datasets, we computed intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs, model ICC\[2,1\]) for all 62 features in both SPH and PTB-XL. Feature-level ICCs were strongly correlated between the two datasets (Spearman ρ \= 0.833, p \< 0.001; **Fig. 3C**), indicating consistent ranking of feature reliability across independent cohorts. Morphological and temporal features tended to show higher reproducibility than more classic interval features in both datasets. For example, R height and RP amplitude difference achieved ICCs \> 0.95 in both SPH and PTB-XL, while interval features such as QT and RR intervals reached ICCs of 0.75–0.85. These values reflect excellent to good within-subject reliability, with most variation attributable to differences between individuals rather than recording noise. 

To further characterize reliability, we ranked the top five features within each group (morphological, temporal, interval) based on ICC estimates in SPH (**Fig. 3D**, *left*). Most of the highest-ranked morphological and temporal features achieved ICCs above 0.90, while top-ranked interval features were lower, in the 0.70–0.85 range. Confidence intervals for these ICCs were narrow (\< ±0.03 in most cases), reflecting stable estimates across subjects. Feature-level coefficients of variation (CVs) supported this pattern (**Fig. 3D**, *right*). Morphological features had the highest average CV (mean ± SD \= 0.061 ± 0.013), followed by interval features (0.043 ± 0.016) and temporal features (0.036 ± 0.005). Group-level variability differed (Kruskal–Wallis *H* \= 7.44, *p* \= 0.024), with post hoc comparisons showing that morphological features were more variable than temporal features (Dunn’s test, p \= 0.033). No significant difference was observed between interval and temporal CVs after correction. Together, these results demonstrate that core ECG features are not only reproducible within subjects but also show consistent reliability patterns across datasets, with morphological features being most reliable in rank but also most variable in absolute terms.

To assess whether ECG features changed across sessions, we applied Wilcoxon signed-rank tests to all features, comparing values between timepoints within each subject. After false discovery rate (FDR) correction, no feature showed significant session-to-session differences (all adjusted p \> 0.99). The most stable features by raw p-value included P rise, T height, and R center (all p \> 0.98), which also ranked highly by ICC and coefficient of variation. The least stable features: Q right voltage, Q decay, and R decay, showed nominal p-values between 0.049 and 0.17, but none survived multiple comparison correction. Effect sizes across features were small, with a median absolute rank-biserial correlation below 0.05, further supporting the temporal stability of ECG feature extraction.

To test whether ECG feature profiles remained person-specific over time, we computed Euclidean distances between session-level feature vectors for the same subject (within-subject). Subsequently, we compared them to distances between different subjects (between-subject) (**Fig. 3E**). Within-subject distances were smaller (z \= –7.85, p \< 0.001, Wilcoxon rank-sum), with a large effect size (Cohen’s d \= 1.22). This result confirms that ECG morphology and timing features remained distinct enough to differentiate individuals across sessions, supporting their utility in personalized modeling and longitudinal tracking.

**Temporal Validation: Within-Session**

To quantify systematic drift within recordings, we compared the average of the first 10 and last 10 beats for each subject (AA: beats 1–10 vs 830–839, n \= 895; MGH: beats 1–10 vs 3853–3862, n \= 183). The window sizes were chosen to reduce noise from any single beat while ensuring coverage at the start and end of each recording; the late beat index was dataset-specific, set to the maximum cycle index available in ≥80% of subjects. In both cohorts, atrial features (P-wave voltages and intervals) and conduction measures (PR and QRS intervals) were stable, showing negligible change across the session (see **Supplementary Table 2**). By contrast, repolarization features exhibited reproducible late-session shifts. In AA, the largest effects were observed in T-wave sharpness (–0.23, adjusted p \< 0.001, T duration (+2.2 ms, adjusted p \< 0.001), and QT interval (+0.6 ms, adjusted p \< 0.001). MGH showed similar patterns, with significant drifts in R rise (–0.83, adjusted p \< 0.001), R duration (–1.1, adjusted p \< 0.001), and S center (+0.14, adjusted p \= 0.02). These results indicate that while depolarization features remain consistent within sessions, repolarization features undergo systematic and measurable drift across the course of longer recordings.

We assessed within-session reliability using single-measure intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC\[A,1\], two-way mixed effects) in the healthy aging (AA; n \= 1,107) and clinical (MGH; n \= 228\) datasets. In AA, the most reliable features were R center voltage (R volt; ICC \= 0.999), R center (0.999), R duration (0.992), T sharpness (0.987), and T center (0.984) (**Fig. 4A, top**). The least reliable were all morphological heights (T, P, Q, S, R; ICC \= 0.40–0.58) (**Fig. 4A, bottom**). MGH showed the same pattern, with R center, T center, R center voltage, S center, and R sharpness all \>0.99, and the lowest ICCs observed for height metrics and the P rise-to-decay ratio (0.29–0.52) (**Fig. 4B**). These results indicate timing and position features are stable, while amplitude features are more variable. Quartile trajectories supported these differences (**Fig. 4C–D**). High-ICC features (R volt, R center, T center) remained flat across quartiles, centered on subject means. Low-ICC features (P, T, R height) also appeared flat, but slope tests revealed small though significant deviations (q \< 0.05; r \= 0.05–0.20). T sharpness in AA showed the only notable drift (median slope ≈ –0.054, r \= 0.68).

Dispersion measures further distinguished feature types. In AA, amplitude features had higher normalized median absolute deviations (MAD \= 0.14–0.21) than temporal ones (\<0.03). MGH showed a similar contrast (S height \= 0.14 vs. R center \= 0.002). Dispersion was greater in AA than MGH overall (median MAD 0.0899 vs. 0.0407; p \< 0.001), suggesting higher beat-to-beat variability in healthy aging.

Agreement plots were used to visualize within-session agreement between early- and late-recording estimates of each feature, not method comparison. Narrow limits of agreement (±0.02 mV or ±10 ms) indicated strong temporal stability for high-ICC features, while amplitude-based metrics showed wider dispersion (\>±0.25 mV; **Fig. 4E–F**). Quartile coefficient of dispersion (QCD) heatmaps showed the same pattern: temporal features had low variability (QCD 0.00–0.04), while morphological heights reached up to 0.22 in AA (**Fig. 4G**). Group-level analysis confirmed temporal features were less variable than morphological ones (p \= 0.033), with MGH showing similar results (**Fig. 4H**). Together, these findings show that timing-based ECG metrics are repeatable within sessions, while normalized amplitude features are less reliable due to greater beat-to-beat dispersion.

**Age-related Modeling**

Among healthy subjects, several ECG features showed robust age-related changes (**Fig. 5A**). Comparisons between younger (\<30 years) and older (≥60 years) adults in the NORM-only cohort revealed marked physiological shifts. We replicated well-known beat-to-beat RR interval variability, which decreased with age (median CV: 0.043 vs. 0.017; Spearman ρ \= −0.62, p \< 0.001), indicating reduced heart rate variability. T-wave repolarization voltage also declined (0.053 vs. 0.042 mV; r \= −0.28, p \< 0.001), while R-wave height variability increased with age (0.126 vs. 0.161; r \= \+0.13, p \< 0.001). Conduction intervals lengthened, with older participants exhibiting longer ST segments (133 vs. 144 ms; r \= \+0.10, p \< 0.001) and QT intervals (369 vs. 394 ms; r \= \+0.34, p \< 0.001). Together, these findings highlight consistent age-related remodeling in both cardiac timing and morphology.

Predictive performance for age modeling in the pooled healthy cohort reached R2 \= 0.441 with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 9.10 years (**Fig. 5B**). Subgroup models performed similarly by sex, with R2 values of 0.418 for males and 0.439 for females, and MAEs of 8.92 and 9.35 years, respectively (**Table 2**). Dataset-level accuracy showed notable variation. SPH (R2 \= 0.392, MAE \= 8.86 yr) and AA (R2 \= 0.343, MAE \= 8.35 yr) achieved moderate performance. PTB-XL, despite its larger sample size, had higher prediction error (MAE \= 10.75 yr) and stronger explained variance (R2 \= 0.421), suggesting greater within-dataset variability. MGH, which included the smallest analytic sample, showed the weakest performance (R2 \= 0.062, MAE \= 12.76 yr), consistent with unstable estimates in small datasets. These results underscore that model accuracy reflects not only dataset size, but also internal variability and cohort characteristics.

Feature attribution using both ablation and permutation methods revealed that beat-to-beat variability accounted for about half of the model’s predictive power (**Fig. 5C–D**). The RR interval coefficient of variation (CV) emerged as the most important individual feature, producing the largest increase in MAE when removed. Morphological features of the QRS complex, such as R height and R width, contributed \~25% of the predictive signal. T-wave and P-wave morphology added smaller but meaningful gains, while conduction intervals such as the QT and ST segments contributed minimally. This distribution suggests that moment-to-moment variability and ventricular morphology are the strongest ECG correlates of biological aging.

Cross-dataset calibration analyses revealed distinct patterns of prediction bias (**Fig. 5E–G**). In the AA dataset, model predictions underestimated chronological age across the full range (**Fig. 5E–F**). In contrast, PTB-XL showed systematic overestimation among younger participants, resulting in a steeper calibration curve early in the age distribution. Predictions in MGH displayed poor fit with a flattened regression slope, consistent with the model's weak performance in this cohort. Residual distributions (**Fig. 5G**) further confirmed dataset-specific error patterns: AA exhibited negatively skewed residuals, PTB-XL showed upward bias in younger age bins, and MGH had wide, dispersed errors. These results emphasize that while the age model captures global patterns of ECG-based aging, its calibration varies by dataset, likely reflecting differences in signal quality, demographic distribution, and sample size.

Bin-wise statistical testing revealed significant differences in absolute prediction error across datasets, particularly involving the AA cohort. In early adulthood (15–30 years), AA showed markedly higher MAEs than both SPH and PTB-XL (all q \< 0.001, FDR-corrected; see **Supplementary Table 3**). Similar differences persisted into midlife (35–60 years), with AA less accurate than SPH and PTB-XL (**Fig. 5H**). Occasional but weaker discrepancies were observed between SPH and PTB-XL (e.g., 25–30 years, q \= 0.023; 35–40 years, q \< 0.01). AA also differed from MGH in the 55–60 year bin (q \< 0.01). Collectively, these results indicate that prediction error is not uniformly distributed across datasets, with AA driving most of the between-cohort differences.

**Mouse** 

To test the adaptability of PyHEARTS to high-frequency cardiac dynamics, we applied the framework to baseline ECG recordings from anesthetized mice (**Fig. 6A–C**). The algorithm accurately detected R peaks across multiple rapid cycles (**Fig. 6A**), and identified all major waveform components within individual beats, including the P, Q, R, S, and T waves (**Fig. 6B**). Feature extraction returned consistent distributions of temporal and morphological metrics such as P rise time, Q sharpness, R rise-to-decay ratio, S duration, and R decay (**Fig. 6C**). These results show that PyHEARTS can effectively segment and parameterize murine ECG signals, even under fast-cycle conditions.

Gaussian fitting yielded high cycle-level reconstruction fidelity, with R2 values clustered near 1.0 (**Fig. 6D**). Empirical cumulative distribution functions (ECDFs) showed that the vast majority of beats exceeded both the 0.95 and 0.99 thresholds (**Fig. 6E**), indicating accurate waveform fitting. The distribution of minus log base ten of one minus R2 values further emphasized this tight clustering (**Fig. 6F**). Root mean square error (RMSE) distributions, visualized via ECDFs, confirmed that reconstruction error remained below one millisecond (**Fig. 6G**). These results demonstrate that PyHEARTS maintains high fidelity when modeling murine ECG signals and supports robust cross-species comparisons.

**Discussion**

Electrocardiography (ECG) remains one of the most widely used tools in cardiology and physiology, yet most analytic pipelines reduce signals to summary metrics such as heart rate, heart rate variability, and conduction intervals measured from a single representative beat. These approaches discard beat-to-beat variability that reflects dynamic physiological processes, including autonomic regulation, aging, and disease risk.. Recent deep learning models recover predictive power from raw ECG signals, including models incorporating post-hoc explainability techniques. However, these approaches primarily provide insight into model behavior rather than producing physiologically grounded representations of cardiac dynamics, which can limit their utility for mechanistic interpretation and translational generalization. Rather than replacing established delineation algorithms, PyHEARTS extends them by retaining beat-level morphological structure and enabling downstream analyses that are not possible with landmark-only outputs.

To address these limitations, we developed PyHEARTS, an algorithmic framework for beat-level ECG feature extraction. PyHEARTS provides physiologically grounded, interpretable features from each cardiac cycle, enabling large-scale modeling of morphology, timing, and variability. Across nearly three million heartbeats from four human cohorts, along with validation in murine recordings, PyHEARTS achieved high reconstruction fidelity and consistent performance across time, datasets, and species. This framework redefines ECG as a high-resolution source of physiological insight, suitable for mechanistic discovery, translational modeling, and data-driven medicine. Unlike traditional ECG delineation approaches that focus on identifying discrete fiducial points, PyHEARTS provides a generative, beat-level parameterization of waveform morphology and timing, enabling continuous characterization of variability across long recordings. This complements classical delineation methods by extending analysis beyond landmark detection to physiologically interpretable morphology and dynamics.

*Reconstruction fidelity and feature stability*

PyHEARTS reconstructed individual ECG cycles with high fidelity. Most beats across all datasets exceeded an R2 threshold of 0.9, with fidelity highest in SPH and PTB-XL, moderate in AA, and lowest in MGH. These differences likely reflect variation in acquisition quality and clinical context, yet the overall pattern demonstrates that the method generalizes well across heterogeneous real-world data.

Feature reproducibility was similarly robust. High-amplitude components such as the R wave and RP difference (R–P amplitude difference)RP difference remained stable both within and between sessions. In contrast, low-amplitude deflections like Q and S voltages showed more variability, particularly in longer recordings with signal drift or subtle changes in sensor position. Amplitude and shape-related metrics are inherently sensitive to electrode placement, skin impedance, and device-specific gain or filtering, all of which can distort absolute voltage even when timing remains precise. This explains why models trained on raw ECG amplitude often fail to generalize across datasets or hardware platforms. By separating acquisition-sensitive morphological features from timing-based physiological features, PyHEARTS makes explicit the sources of variability that are implicitly entangled in end-to-end deep learning models. In contrast, temporal landmarks such as onset, offset, and duration are less affected by these factors and therefore more transferable. These patterns highlight a key advantage of beat-level parameterization: separating morphology that reflects acquisition-dependent variance from timing-based physiology that generalizes across individuals, sessions, and sensors.

Among all components, the T wave showed the greatest beat-to-beat variability in amplitude and sharpness. This contrasted with the stability of timing-based metrics such as QT interval or R peak position. These fluctuations in repolarization morphology likely reflect autonomic modulation or metabolic state, rather than noise. Prior studies have linked T-wave heterogeneity to arrhythmic risk, but few tools quantify such variation at the cycle level. By capturing this variability directly, PyHEARTS distinguishes between structural features that remain stable and dynamic signals that reflect changing physiological states. This distinction is essential for emerging applications such as stress monitoring, circadian tracking, or state-dependent biomarker development.

*Biological aging and predictive modeling*

Age prediction was used here as a representative downstream task to assess the informativeness and stability of PyHEARTS-derived features, rather than as an attempt to optimize predictive accuracy. Thus, hHaving established signal fidelity and reproducibility, we next evaluated whether PyHEARTS could capture physiological changes associated with aging. Despite using only linear models, PyHEARTS achieved a mean absolute error of approximately 9 years, which falls within the range reported for deep learning–based ECG age models in prior studiesachieved age prediction accuracy on par with state-of-the-art deep learning approaches. The mean absolute error was approximately 9 years, with no significant loss of performance in sex-stratified models. However, direct numerical comparison across studies is limited by differences in cohorts, preprocessing, and modeling objectives. This result demonstrates that interpretable, physiologically grounded features can support competitive predictive performance without requiring complex end-to-end AI architectures, particularly when the goal is mechanistic insight rather than maximal accuracy.This result challenges the assumption that high prediction accuracy requires complex AI architectures, and highlights the potential of interpretable models built from physiologically interpretable features.

Model interpretation revealed two distinct trends in cardiac aging. First, beat-to-beat variability declined with age, consistent with reduced autonomic flexibility. Second, conduction intervals such as ST and QT increased later in life, consistent with structural remodeling and reduced conduction efficiency. This pattern suggests that aging involves both gradual shifts in regulatory control and discrete transitions linked to loss of compensatory capacity.

Variability features contributed nearly half of the predictive signal, with RR interval variability emerging as the strongest individual feature. This dominance is consistent with known age-related reductions in autonomic flexibility and does not diminish the value of morphological features, which provided complementary information and are likely more informative for other clinical and physiological endpoints. Morphological metrics related to QRS and T-wave shape added complementary value, while conventional conduction intervals contributed less. These results align with prior findings that autonomic dysregulation often precedes overt structural disease, and position variability metrics as early, interpretable markers of biological aging. The growing field of ECG-based biological age estimation underscores how morphological and temporal features capture cardiovascular aging and systemic health[39](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Wp1MFv).

Prediction performance varied across datasets, driven by differences in signal quality and cohort composition. Our model achieved moderate performance on the SPH and AA datasets, while there was a systematic calibration bias evident in its performance on PTB-XL. It performed relatively poorly on the MGH dataset, likely due to its small, heterogeneous sample. These differences underscore the importance of acquisition protocols, demographic context, and dataset curation in model performance.

*Cross-species generalization*

Remarkably, Wwith few modifications PyHEARTS generalizesd to murine ECG, despite much faster heart rates and shorter cardiac cycles in mice. The pipeline segmented beats, identified all major deflections, and achieved sub-millisecond reconstruction error. This establishes PyHEARTS as a cross-species analysis framework that enables standardized comparison between human and animal data. Such capability is critical for translational research in aging, autonomic function, and electrophysiologic disease.

*Modularity and extensibility* 

Beyond core feature extraction, PyHEARTS was designed for flexible use and integration. Its modular structure allows users to apply the full pipeline or select subsets of features. It can be combined with ML models, time-series embeddings, or interactive diagnostic workflows. As a resource, it supports reproducibility and fosters adoption across domains including cardiology, neuroscience, physiology, and digital health.

*Limitations and future directions*

While exciting, our study has several limitations. Beat-level feature extraction increases sensitivity to noise, especially in low-amplitude waves such as Q and S. Although SNR filtering reduces false positives, recordings with poor quality may result in poor interpretability or require exclusion entirely. While our analyses were limited to four public datasets with different lead configurations and clinical populations, its success on these data supports its generalizability but limits conclusions about underrepresented physiological contexts. The current implementation emphasizes Gaussian fitting and predefined features, which may not capture nonlinear or pathological waveform dynamics. While physiological relevance and reproducibility were demonstrated, we did not evaluate clinical outcomes such as mortality, arrhythmia, or response to treatment. Finally, species validation was limited to humans and mice.

These limitations point to clear opportunities for future work, however. Clinical studies could assess the prognostic utility of PyHEARTS features for patient stratification, treatment monitoring, or real-time diagnosis. Longitudinal data could characterize how variability patterns evolve across the lifespan or in disease progression. Integrating interpretable ML may further enhance predictive performance without sacrificing transparency. Extension to arrhythmic conditions and other model organisms would strengthen translational applications and broaden generalizability.

Importantly, PyHEARTS is not intended to replace deep learning or explainable AI approaches, but rather to provide a physiology-centric representation that can be used independently or integrated with machine learning models to improve interpretability, robustness, and translational relevance.

*Conclusion*

PyHEARTS offers a reproducible, interpretable, and high-resolution framework for ECG feature extraction. It preserves beat-level morphology and timing, enabling accurate and consistent modeling across datasets, sessions, and species. By recovering variability that is typically discarded or obscured, PyHEARTS repositions ECG as a rich signal source for physiological modeling, precision phenotyping, and translational research.

Variability features emerged as sensitive indicators of biological aging and autonomic regulation, while temporal and morphological metrics offered complementary stability. The ability to extract these features at scale, without requiring black-box models, opens new directions for biomarker development, personalized monitoring, and clinical prediction. Adoption of frameworks like PyHEARTS may accelerate the integration of electrophysiology into data-driven medicine and support the development of digital twins for cardiac physiology.
