**Methods**

**Software Overview**

PyHEARTS is a Python toolbox for automated beat-wise analysis of single-lead ECG recordings. An overview of the full processing pipeline is shown in Figure 1\. It extracts a comprehensive set of morphological, temporal, and interval-based features from each detected cardiac cycle. These include wave amplitudes and durations, fiducial latencies, conduction intervals (e.g., PR, QRS, QT), and heart rate variability (HRV) metrics (see **Supplementary Table 1** for full list).

Each beat is processed independently, and results are output as a structured pandas.DataFrame, with one row per cycle. Sample indices and millisecond-resolved timestamps are recorded for all detected events, enabling traceability between raw signals and derived features. All processed outputs are saved to CSV, alongside a serialized configuration object (ProcessCycleConfig; **Supplementary** **Table 4**) that defines all parameters used during analysis. This ensures reproducibility and facilitates reanalysis.

PyHEARTS supports human and mouse ECG recordings with species-specific presets. All parameters, such as detection thresholds, filter settings, and morphological criteria, were defined via the ProcessCycleConfig object. This configuration schema allowed consistent and transparent application of physiological constraints across all ECG records analyzed. Finally, the toolbox requires only standard Python libraries (NumPy, SciPy, pandas) and runs on signals with a minimum of two cardiac cycles with traceable R-peaks.

*Parameter Configuration*

All thresholds and parameter defaults in ProcessCycleConfig were chosen based on general physiological plausibility. Physiological limits (e.g., RR interval bounds, wave duration minima, polarity expectations) reflect field-established ranges for both human and murine ECGs. Parameters without clear physiological constraints (e.g., peak detection prominence factors, quality thresholds, curve-fitting bounds) were tuned empirically using the AA and PTB-XL datasets to ensure robust behavior across a broad spectrum of signal conditions and demographic diversity. Full configuration defaults are in ProcessCycleConfig, with species-specific presets available via for\_human() and for\_mouse().

### *Datasets*

We validated PyHEARTS on four human ECG datasets comprising 32,191 recordings from 30,686 subjects, totaling over 2.9 million beats (**Table 1**). These datasets spanned a wide age range (0 to 100 years), included both healthy and clinical populations, and varied in recording duration, sampling rate, and annotation protocols. All signals were analyzed as single-lead traces, with lead II selected across all datasets. In the rare event that lead II was corrupted or unavailable, lead I was used as a fallback to preserve morphological consistency.

The Autonomic Aging (AA) dataset consisted of resting ECGs sampled at 1,000 Hz from 1,121 healthy adults aged 18 to 85 years (mean age: 32.5). Recordings lasted between 8 and 35 minutes and did not include diagnostic labels.

The Physikalisch Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB-XL) dataset comprised 5,050 ECGs from 4,649 patients, each sampled at 500 Hz and lasting 10 seconds. Note that due to sampling rate requirements (see Sampling Rate section), we were limited to the high-resolution (500 Hz) subset of PTB-XL. Subjects ranged in age from 0 to 95 years (mean: 62.0), and each recording included physician-assigned diagnostic labels.

The Shandong Provincial Hospital (SPH) Clinical Dataset included 25,770 ECGs from 24,666 patients, with a mean age of 50.7 years. Recordings ranged from 10 to 60 seconds in duration and were sampled at 500 Hz. Diagnostic annotations followed standard American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines.

The Massachusetts General Hospital/Marquette Foundation (MGH) Waveform Database contained 250 recordings from 250 individuals aged 1 to 88 years (mean: 58.7), with sampling at 360 Hz. Record durations ranged from 12 to 86 minutes. Clinical labels were available and used where applicable.

*Mouse Data*

To evaluate cross-species compatibility of the analysis pipeline, baseline ECG recordings were acquired from 13 adult C57BL/6J mice (1.5–6 months old, both sexes) under light isoflurane anesthesia (1.0–1.5% in oxygen)[53](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?zrxIuW), in accordance with protocols approved by the Scripps Research IACUC. Signals were recorded using subcutaneous needle electrodes in lead I configuration at a sampling rate of 3,000 Hz (PowerLab, ADInstruments), selected to ensure accurate capture of fast murine cardiac dynamics. No randomization or blinding was performed.

*Preprocessing*

All ECG signals were preprocessed using a standardized filtering pipeline. A high-pass filter at 0.5 Hz was applied to remove baseline drift, implemented as a 4th-order zero-phase Butterworth filter using forward–backward filtering to preserve phase. Notch filtering was applied at regional mains interference (MGH: 60 Hz; AA, PTB-XL, SPH: 50 Hz). 

*Sampling Rate*

Accurate ECG feature extraction requires sufficient temporal resolution to capture sharp waveform components. Although the Nyquist criterion sets a lower bound of two samples per cycle, reliable detection of deflections like the Q and S waves (lasting as little as 20–40 ms) typically requires at least six samples to preserve waveform morphology and allow precise localization of boundaries. This corresponds to a minimum sampling rate of \~300 Hz. Similar thresholds are supported in signal processing literature[54](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?rUBHc8), and all human datasets used in this study exceeded this: AA (1,000 Hz), SPH/PTB-XL (500 Hz), and MGH (360 Hz).

In mice, the physiological constraints are more demanding. Murine QRS complexes are typically shorter than 10 milliseconds, with Q and S waves often lasting only 2 to 4 milliseconds. These features contain frequency components in the several-hundred-Hz range. To prevent aliasing and enable reliable sub-millisecond curve fitting, we required a minimum sampling rate of 2,500 Hz for murine ECGs. All mouse recordings used in this study were sampled at or above 3,000 Hz, ensuring fidelity in waveform reconstruction.

*Cycle Segmentation*

R-peak detection was performed using a two-pass, prominence-based algorithm implemented with scipy.signal.find\_peaks. 

In the first pass, a permissive refractory period was applied to exclude physiologically implausible peak intervals: 120 milliseconds for the human preset and 67 milliseconds for the mouse preset. These thresholds correspond to theoretical maximum heart rates of approximately 500 beats per minute (bpm) and 900 bpm, respectively[24,54,55](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?fWQalC). This is based on the formula: 60,000 ms/min divided by the RR interval in milliseconds. For example, 60,000 ÷ 120 ms \= 500 bpm, and 60,000 ÷ 67 ms ≈ 896 bpm. 

The human threshold exceeds typical maximum sinus rates observed during exertion (about 200–220 bpm), allowing a wide margin that helps reject noise while preserving true beats, including rare tachycardic episodes[56–59](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?hMCuqR). The mouse threshold accounts for reported peak physiological rates under stress (around 700–800 bpm), with additional headroom for transient extremes[55,60,61](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?udD0jZ). These values support the use of a theoretical upper limit for artifact rejection during R-peak detection. Prominence was set adaptively based on the standard deviation of the signal (prominence \= 3.0 times the signal’s standard deviation), allowing sensitivity to adjust according to the noise level in each recording[62,63](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?P46Uz1).

In the second pass, a refined search was conducted using a dynamic refractory period equal to 55% of the estimated median RR interval, with RR estimates constrained to species-specific physiological ranges (30–240 bpm for humans, 300–1000 bpm for mice)[55,56,61,62,64–66](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?9tOaZ2). These bounds reflect published limits on sinus rhythm and reduce the risk of artifactual RR values skewing cycle segmentation. Only peaks identified in the second pass were retained for downstream analysis.

Epoching and cycle screening were performed around each detected R peak. A symmetric window was extracted for each beat, with a half-width equal to half the average RR interval for that recording. This ensured full-cycle coverage centered on each R-wave. Each cycle was subjected to two quality checks. First, the beat had to correlate with the global average cycle at ≥0.80. Second, its variance could not exceed five times that of the full trace. Cycles passing both thresholds were retained and indexed for downstream analysis.

Per-cycle baseline and trend removal was then applied. Each beat was corrected in two stages. A baseline offset was removed by subtracting the median voltage of the initial portion of the cycle, defined as the first 200 ms for human signals and 100 ms for murine signals. Then, the linear trend for each cycle was found by fitting a line between the first and last sample of the cycle, and this trend was subtracted. The resulting detrended waveform and slope estimate (cycle\_trend) were stored for each beat and served as the foundation for all subsequent steps, including peak localization and morphological fitting.

### *Peak Detection*

PyHEARTS does not assume the presence of all PQRST components in every beat. Unlike classical delineators that estimate fiducial points using fixed windows or global templates, PyHEARTS initializes search regions using physiological priors but adapts them on a per-beat basis using signal-derived features. Candidate P, Q, S, and T waves are evaluated independently using existence, polarity, and amplitude-based validation criteria. If a component cannot be reliably detected within its search window, fails validation, or is physiologically implausible (e.g., absent P wave, low SNR, inverted polarity under the default lead assumption), that component is omitted and its corresponding fiducial and morphology features are recorded as missing (NaN) rather than forced. Gaussian fitting is performed conditionally only for validated components, and failure of one component does not prevent extraction of others within the same beat. Beats with partial component sets are retained for downstream analysis, while analyses requiring a specific component (e.g., PR interval requires P onset) operate only on beats where the required fiducials are present.

Candidate P, Q, R, S, and T waves were identified from detrended ECG waveform using a rule-based approach grounded in signal morphology and timing. For each beat, QRS boundaries were initialized symmetrically around the R peak using a window of ±1.75σ, where σ was computed from the full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) of the R deflection. This base estimate was then dynamically expanded using wavelet-guided offsets. 

Discrete wavelet detail coefficients were calculated using a Daubechies-6 (db6) wavelet, with the decomposition level determined by the length of the signal. Peaks in the absolute value of these coefficients that exceeded 1.2 times the signal’s standard deviation were aggregated per beat to form a QRS energy proxy. This threshold (1.2σ) was chosen to balance sensitivity and specificity, based on the expected amplitude distribution of wavelet-transformed ECGs. Prior work in ECG delineation has used similar σ-based thresholds (typically 1.0–1.5σ[67](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?IwFaKm)) to isolate depolarization-related energy while suppressing background noise. 

Search windows are initialized using physiological priors but are adjusted on a per-beat basis using signal-derived features, including R-peak width (via FWHM), wavelet energy localization, and recording-specific RR intervals. This allows fiducial localization to adapt to atypical morphologies (e.g., broad QRS, delayed repolarization, variable PR timing) without assuming normal sinus rhythm.

To tailor the analysis to each beat, waveform amplitude strength was quantified and normalized to the 95th percentile of the record. This measure was then linearly mapped to define a beat-specific offset between 1 and 60 milliseconds. The adaptive offset adjusts how far before and after the initial QRS bounds the algorithm searches for the Q and S wave peaks. Beats with larger overall amplitudes receive wider search zones, while lower-amplitude beats receive narrower ones. Although this offset does not represent total QRS duration, it allows the search region to extend beyond 125 milliseconds, consistent with durations observed in healthy rhythms[68](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?PzVdCv). 

The Q wave was defined as the most negative deflection in the interval from the left QRS bound up to, but not including, the R peak. The S wave was defined as the most negative deflection between the R peak and the right QRS bound. If the right bound extended beyond the available signal, it was clamped to 100 samples before the boundary to avoid indexing errors during downstream processing.

P wave detection occurred before the QRS complex, within a window defined by the most positive peak between a start index and the beginning of the QRS. The end of the window was set to the Q wave if present, otherwise to the R peak. The start index was chosen as the earliest of either approximately 10 milliseconds from the start of the cycle. This approach ensured that even in longer pre-QRS intervals, the search window remained bounded and physiologically meaningful.

T wave detection began after a fixed post-QRS guard interval (postQRS\_refractory\_window\_ms), which separated the T-wave search region from residual depolarization in the S-wave tail. This guard reduced false detections near the QRS offset. The interval was set to 10 ms for murine ECGs and 20 ms for human ECGs, reflecting species-specific timing: in mice, T waves typically begin 20–30 ms after the R peak, whereas in humans they appear 40–80 ms after the QRS complex[68](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?OutG69). The T-wave search window extended from the end of this guard interval up to half the detrending window length, ensuring that detection remained within the same cardiac cycle and excluded baseline drift or the onset of the next P wave.

Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) gating was applied to P and T waves to improve robustness in lower-amplitude regions of the ECG. These waves are more vulnerable to noise from breathing, motion artifacts, and low-frequency drift, and lack the strong polarity and timing cues that define the QRS complex. Q and S waves were not gated, since they could be reliably located based on their expected shape and proximity to the R peak.

For P waves, noise was estimated using a rolling median absolute deviation (MAD), excluding a window equal to the FWHM around the candidate peak. No smoothing was used in P wave detection. For T waves, additional constraints and filtering were required due to their lower amplitude, broader duration, and greater susceptibility to baseline drift compared with depolarization components[69–71](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?zo4WuY). The local noise estimate was computed using a fixed exclusion window centered on the candidate (±20 ms for mice, ±10 ms for humans) to avoid contamination from the repolarization slope. This window size reflects the typical width of the T apex region in each species, ensuring noise is sampled from the nearby baseline rather than the repolarization phase itself. When the configuration flag snr\_apply\_savgol\["T"\] was enabled, a Savitzky–Golay filter was applied to the detrended signal only for apex smoothing. This step reduced high-frequency fluctuations that otherwise distort the T-peak position in noisy recordings while preserving true morphology. In all cases, amplitude values used for gating and polarity assessment were extracted directly from the unfiltered detrended waveform to maintain physiological fidelity. Candidate P and T waves were retained only if their absolute amplitude exceeded a configurable multiple of the MAD, using the formula: |peak| ≥ k × MAD, where the value of k was set using the snr\_mad\_multiplier parameter. Typical values were 2.0 for mice and 1.75 to 2.0 for humans. Waves with inverted polarity (negative) in standard ECG leads, such as lead II, were excluded from analysis.

To ensure valid cardiac cycle detection, R-peak detection was constrained by species-specific physiological heart rate ranges. For mice, this range was 300 to 1000 beats per minute (bpm), corresponding to minimum R–R intervals of 67 milliseconds. For humans, the acceptable range was 30 to 240 bpm, with a minimum interval of 120 milliseconds. These bounds helped avoid mislabeling overlapping P, T, or R waves, supported accurate cycle labeling, and ensured valid measurement of durations and wave morphologies.

Candidate P, Q, S, and T peaks were further validated using three criteria: existence, polarity, and R-normalized amplitude. Validation was not applied to R peaks, which served as the cycle reference. First, peaks were excluded if their index was missing or their amplitude was not finite. Second, polarity was checked based on standard lead II morphology: P and T waves were required to be positive, Q and S negative. In other leads with inverted morphology, polarity must be adjusted or the signal inverted upstream, or the candidate will be rejected. For datasets with known inverted polarity, alternate lead placement, or frequent biphasic waves, users can invert the signal or adjust polarity expectations in the configuration; otherwise, components violating polarity constraints are treated as absent and omitted.

Third, peak amplitude was compared to the same-cycle R amplitude, if available and finite. Peaks were retained only if |peak| ≥ α × |R|, where α \= amp\_min\_ratio\[component\]. These thresholds were drawn from ProcessCycleConfig and matched species-specific presets. For humans, defaults were: P ≥ 0.03, T ≥ 0.05, Q and S ≥ 0.02 × |R|. For mice: P ≥ 0.03, T ≥ 0.04, Q and S ≥ 0.025 × |R|. These values were chosen to sit above the typical noise floor while preserving small physiological deflections. All amplitude comparisons used the detrended, unsmoothed signal, regardless of whether smoothing was used during detection.

Peaks failing any validation step were set to (None, None) and excluded from Gaussian fitting and shape-feature extraction in downstream analysis.

*Gaussian Fitting*

Gaussian fitting is performed conditionally for each waveform component and only when that component has passed peak detection and validation. Initial fitting was performed without seeding when no valid parameters were available from a previous cycle.Initial Gaussian fitting was performed without seeding when no valid parameters were available from a previous cycle. For each validated deflection (P, Q, R, S, T), Gaussian parameters were initialized from the detrended ECG signal. The center was set to the detected peak index, the amplitude to the signal value at that index, and the width (σ) was estimated from the full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) using the standard conversion: σ \= FWHM / 2.3548. A minimum σ of 0.5 samples was enforced to avoid instability in narrow or low-amplitude peaks.

Waveforms were fitted using nonlinear least-squares optimization (scipy.optimize.curve\_fit) with the trust-region reflective algorithm. Bounds were defined as ±20% around the initial estimates of center, amplitude, and σ (bound\_factor \= 0.20). Amplitude bounds were centered on the signed initial guess, which preserves waveform polarity and ensures that negative waves (e.g., Q and S) remain negative during optimization. The solver was allowed up to 2,500 function evaluations per fit.

If a valid Gaussian fit existed for a component in the previous cycle, its center, amplitude, and σ were used as the initial guess. Bounds were recomputed using the same ±20% factor, and all guesses were clamped within those limits. If the seeded fit succeeded, its parameters were used for the next beat; otherwise, the algorithm fell back to the unseeded path.

After fitting, the Gaussian center was refined by snapping to the nearest local extremum in the detrended signal. This step ensured that the reported peak corresponded to the true voltage apex of the measured waveform, rather than the theoretical maximum of the fitted curve. Because Gaussian fits can slightly misalign with the actual peak, especially in asymmetric or noisy waves, the snapping correction anchors the model to the empirical signal. The snapping window was ±(half-FWHM) for seeded fits, based on the fitted σ, or a fixed ±10-sample window for unseeded fits. Final gaussian parameters (center, amplitude, σ, and computed FWHM \= (2ln(2)) were stored in both sample and millisecond units, along with global indices for traceability.

*Feature Extraction*

Morphological features were extracted from the Gaussian-reconstructed ECG signal, defined as the sum of all fitted components. This approach was chosen over using the raw ECG to ensure smooth, noise-robust wave delineation.

For each detected wave (P, Q, R, S, T), onset and offset were defined as the points where the fitted signal fell below 30% of the wave’s peak amplitude. This fixed threshold (threshold\_fraction \= 0.30) was applied with polarity-aware logic: upward crossings for positive deflections (P, R, T) and downward crossings for negative deflections (Q, S). The 30% level was chosen to preserve small but physiologically relevant features such as Q and S waves while avoiding premature truncation at the baseline.

The search for these threshold crossings proceeded outward from the Gaussian peak center, but the maximum search distance was limited in two steps. First, the half-window was scaled to the fitted width of the component, set to twice its standard deviation (shape\_search\_scale \= 2.0). This allowed the window to adapt to broad versus narrow waveforms. Second, this dynamic window was capped by fixed physiologic limits defined separately for each wave type and species (e.g., human T ≤200 ms, mouse T ≤60 ms). This combination ensured that the search was wide enough to capture physiologic morphology but bounded to avoid encroaching into neighboring deflections or noise.

For human data, the P wave window was capped at 160 ms (typical duration 80–110 ms), ≤60 ms for Q and S, ≤80 ms for R (total QRS expected duration 70–110 ms), and the T wave at 200 ms (expected 150–250 ms). For mouse data, reflecting shorter cardiac cycles at 600–800 bpm, the P wave was capped at 35 ms (expected 5–15 ms), the Q and S at ≤12 ms, ≤18 ms for R (expected QRS total 10–20 ms), and the T wave at 60 ms (expected 40–80 ms). This two-tiered policy allowed the delineation window to adapt to the empirical shape of each wave while remaining within physiologically plausible boundaries.

For each component, several morphological features were computed from the fitted signal between the detected onset and offset. These included total duration, rise and decay times (onset to peak and peak to offset, respectively), and rise–decay symmetry, defined as the ratio of rise time to total duration. Sharpness was quantified as the 95th percentile of the first derivative within the wave boundaries, normalized by amplitude; the normalization mode (“peak-to-peak”) used the voltage difference between the component’s maximum and minimum as the scaling factor. This approach provides a consistent, polarity-independent measure of sharpness that accounts for both positive and negative deflections. The voltage integral was computed using trapezoidal integration of the detrended fitted signal within the wave bounds, yielding a measure in microvolt-milliseconds (µV·ms).

Cardiac conduction intervals were derived directly from the onset and offset times of the relevant fitted waves. These included PR, QRS, and QT intervals, along with beat-wise metrics such as peak amplitudes, Gaussian fit parameters, and interdeflection voltage differences. Taken together, these steps defined a reproducible and physiologically grounded pipeline for waveform delineation and feature extraction. A complete list of computed features is provided in **Supplementary Table 1**.

*Fit metrics*

Each Gaussian fit was evaluated using two reconstruction metrics: the squared Pearson correlation coefficient (R2) and the root mean squared error (RMSE), both computed between the detrended ECG signal and the fitted waveform. These metrics quantified how well the Gaussian model approximated the true signal morphology.

A beat was considered successfully parameterized if at least one major component was successfully detected and fit; missing or failed components were handled independently and recorded as missing values, allowing beats with absent P waves or poorly defined T waves to contribute valid QRS- and RR-derived features. A beat was considered successfully parameterized if at least one major waveform component (P, Q, R, S, or T) passed all fitting and shape validation checks. Components that failed were excluded independently, and their associated features were marked as missing. Partial success was permitted, allowing valid components from a given cycle to contribute to downstream analysis even when others failed.

RR and PP intervals were smoothed using a 3-beat moving average and filtered to retain only values within species-specific bounds, as defined in the configuration. This limited smoothing was applied only to RR and PP because these intervals exhibit high beat-to-beat variability due to physiological rhythm fluctuations and detection jitter, both of which can introduce spurious local outliers. Smoothing stabilizes instantaneous rate estimates without distorting true timing trends. In contrast, other interval features (e.g., PR, QT, QRS) describe intra-beat morphology rather than inter-beat timing and are less affected by cycle-to-cycle variability or detector noise; thus, they were left unsmoothed to preserve each beat’s exact waveform geometry. All time-based thresholds and durations were converted to samples using round(ms · fs / 1000), and all processing was governed by a centralized configuration object for reproducibility.

*Heart rate variability*

Heart rate variability (HRV) features were computed from RR intervals using standard time-domain measures: mean heart rate, SDNN, RMSSD, and NN50. These metrics were calculated only when at least 60 valid RR intervals were available. If the threshold was not met, HRV outputs were excluded.

Cardiac cycles were excluded from analysis under the following conditions: missing input data, failure to fit key waveform components, or presence of NaNs in required fields. In cases of partial failure, only the affected features were marked as missing, while valid outputs from the same cycle were retained. 

\----

**Statistical Analysis**

All computations were performed in Python using NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, Pandas and custom modules within the PyHEARTS toolbox. Visualization of results was carried out using matplotlib and seaborn.

*Data Cleaning*

All raw feature tables were processed using a standardized data cleaning pipeline to ensure physiological plausibility and statistical robustness. For each input file, CSVs were read into memory and underwent the following preprocessing steps: (1) Polarity constraints were applied to enforce electrophysiological validity. P, R, and T waves were required to have positive center voltages, while Q and S waves were expected to be negative. Values that violated these sign rules or showed incorrect peak polarity based on Gaussian fits were replaced with missing values (NaN). (2) Outlier removal was performed on all numeric columns with at least 10 valid entries. Values more than three standard deviations from the column mean were marked as NaN. (3) Identifier formatting ensured that the ecg\_id and cycle\_index fields were stored as nullable integers, preserving missing values while maintaining consistency across files. Cleaned files were saved and used in all downstream analyses. Importantly, these plausibility filters do not impute missing components; they only mark implausible component-specific values as missing while retaining other valid features from the same beat.

*Feature Engineering*

To quantify variability in cardiac morphology and timing within each subject, three statistical measures were computed per feature: standard deviation, coefficient of variation, and interquartile range. The standard deviation provided an absolute measure of dispersion across cardiac cycles. The coefficient of variation, defined as the standard deviation divided by the absolute mean, captured relative variability and was suppressed when the mean value fell below machine precision to prevent unstable estimates. The interquartile range, calculated as the difference between the 75th and 25th percentiles, served as a robust non-parametric indicator of spread. Each variability metric was computed independently per feature and appended to the feature table using suffixes indicating the corresponding measure (e.g., \_std, \_cv, \_iqr).

Subject-level features and variability metrics were compiled into a unified table for downstream statistical analysis.

*Dataset Comparisons*

To compare feature distributions across datasets, we used the Kruskal–Wallis test as a non-parametric omnibus comparison. Effect sizes were reported as η2, computed using the formula η2 \= (H − k \+ 1)/(n − k), where *H* is the Kruskal–Wallis test statistic, k is the number of groups, and n is the total number of observations. Pairwise differences were assessed using two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann–Whitney U) tests with asymptotic p-values and tie correction. Multiple comparisons were controlled using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure[72](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?oH76Yg) at q \< 0.05, applied independently within each feature group.

For each pairwise comparison, we reported Cliff’s δ along with 95% confidence intervals derived from 2,000 percentile bootstrap resamples. Median differences between groups were also computed with bootstrap confidence intervals using the same resampling framework. To maintain computational efficiency, large cohorts (n \> 10,000) were randomly downsampled once prior to resampling.

Reconstruction quality was evaluated at the cycle level using three metrics: R2, RMSE, and MAE, calculated within a 600 ms window centered on each R peak, independent of species. The 600 ms threshold was chosen to capture the full morphology of a typical cardiac cycle segment (P wave, QRS complex, and T wave) while avoiding overlap with adjacent beats. Subject-level summaries were computed as the median of cycle-level values, along with the mean and standard deviation of R2, the median and 95th percentile of RMSE, and the median of MAE. Thresholds for high-quality reconstructions were defined as R2 ≥ 0.9, RMSE ≤ 0.1 mV, and MAE ≤ 0.2 mV[47–49](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Fz8nRb). A quadrant-based classification was used to determine the proportion of subjects meeting both fidelity and error criteria.

To compare reconstruction performance across datasets, we used chi-squared tests of independence. Effect sizes for categorical outcomes were reported using Cramér’s V or Cohen’s h, depending on the number of groups being compared. Associations between reconstruction fidelity metrics (e.g., mean R2 vs. 95th percentile RMSE) were quantified using Spearman’s rank correlation (ρ). All statistical tests were two-sided and non-parametric unless otherwise specified.

### **Reliability and Predictive Modeling**

*Between Session* 

We evaluated between-session reliability of ECG features using PTB-XL and SPH. The PTB-XL subset included 294 subjects with at least two valid 500 Hz lead II recordings (588 total ECGs). From SPH, 1,048 subjects had at least two lead II recordings (2,096 total ECGs). For consistency, the first two recordings per subject (lowest ECG identifiers) were selected, and only subjects with complete data from both sessions were retained.

Beat-wise features were extracted using the PyHEARTS pipeline and summarized at the session level by taking the median across beats. Features were grouped into morphological (e.g., voltages, waveform integrals, sharpness), temporal (e.g., durations, rise and decay times, Gaussian centers), and interval-based measures (e.g., PR, QT, RR, PP). Grouping was performed using predefined keyword-based rules applied uniformly across datasets.

Reliability was quantified with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) estimated for each feature using a two-way mixed-effects, absolute-agreement model \[ICC(A,1)\], implemented in the pingouin package. Confidence intervals were obtained using Fisher’s z-transformation. Within each dataset, features were ranked by ICC to identify the most and least stable measures. To evaluate generalizability, ICC rankings from PTB-XL and SPH were compared directly, allowing identification of features that consistently demonstrated high or low reliability across both cohorts. The top- and bottom-ranked features were selected for visualization to illustrate the spectrum of between-session stability.

*Within Session*

To evaluate within-recording stability, we compared feature values between early and late time windows within each ECG recording. A dataset-specific "late" beat index was defined as the largest cycle index present in at least 80% of recordings (AA: 835; MGH: 3,862). The early window consisted of beats 1–10, and the late window included the final 10 beats ending at the dataset-specific late index. Subjects were retained if both windows contained at least six valid beats. For each feature, we computed the average within each window.

To assess change over time, we tested whether the feature values differed between early and late windows using the paired t-test if both distributions passed the D’Agostino test for normality. Otherwise, we used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. We summarized differences as the mean (for t-tests) or median (for Wilcoxon) of the within-subject late-minus-early values. To correct for multiple comparisons across features, we applied the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR), reporting adjusted q-values.

To estimate the within-session test–retest reliability, we computed intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC\[A,1\]) for each ECG feature. This model reflects absolute agreement in a two-way mixed-effects design with a single measurement per phase. Each recording was divided into early and late phases, defined as the first and last deciles of valid beats based on subject-specific beat count. Subjects were included if both phases contained at least six valid beats. No imputation was used; missing beats were excluded listwise within each phase. For each subject and feature, we computed the median value within the early and late phases. ICCs were estimated using pingouin.icc (v0.5.3), specifying a two-way mixed-effects, absolute-agreement model (type \= "ICC2", unit \= "single"). Confidence intervals were computed using Fisher z-transformation, as implemented by the package. We report ICCs, 95% confidence intervals, and the number of subjects contributing to each feature. Axis clipping in visualizations (e.g., bar plots) did not affect ICC computation.

To assess temporal variability across full recordings, we computed quartile coefficients of dispersion (QCD) for each ECG feature. Beats within each subject were first ranked by normalized index r \= (rank − 1\) / (B − 1), where B is the total number of valid beats. Quartile bins were defined as Q1: \[0, 0.25\], Q2: (0.25, 0.5\], Q3: (0.5, 0.75\], Q4: (0.75, 1\], using pandas.cut(...,right=True,include\_lowest=True). Subject–quartile combinations with fewer than two beats were excluded. Subjects with fewer than four total beats were excluded entirely from the analysis. For each subject and feature, QCD was computed separately in each quartile as: QCD \= (Q3 − Q1) / (Q3 \+ Q1), where Q1 and Q3 are the first and third quartiles of the beat-level values within that quartile. If Q3 \+ Q1 \= 0, QCD was set to NaN. Feature-level QCD profiles were then aggregated across subjects by the median, producing a four-column QCD profile (Q1–Q4) per feature. This approach complements the early–late analysis by capturing temporal fluctuations across the entire session rather than only at the endpoints. Using normalized quartiles allows comparisons across subjects with different recording lengths. QCD was chosen over the coefficient of variation for its scale invariance and robustness to non-normal distributions. 

For visualization, features were ranked by ICC(A,1), and QCD heatmaps were plotted for the top five and bottom five features across both datasets. Color limits were fixed based on the global finite minimum and maximum across AA and MGH to enable direct cross-dataset comparison.

***Aging***

To examine the relationship between ECG features and age, we first performed two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests comparing adults under 30 years and those aged 60 and older. Features with significant group differences in morphology, timing, or variability were retained for predictive modeling.

Chronological age was modeled using histogram-based gradient boosting regressors (HistGradientBoostingRegressor, scikit-learn). A five-fold GroupKFold cross-validation was used to avoid subject leakage. Within each fold, features were z-scored based on training data, and low-variance (≤1e–6) or near-duplicate (|r| \> 0.999) features were removed. Standardization and pruning were applied only to training folds to prevent data leakage.

After model training, predictions were calibrated using isotonic regression. Performance was evaluated using out-of-fold (OOF) R2 and mean absolute error (MAE) in years. Subgroup performance was reported by sex and dataset. Linear regression baselines, including ordinary least squares and Ridge regression with tuned α, were fit using the same pipeline for comparison.

Feature importance was estimated using OOF permutation analysis, where the impact of each feature was quantified by its effect on MAE. Grouped ablation tests were used to assess the contribution of different physiological feature sets (e.g., removing variability features). The resulting change in MAE (ΔMAE) was used to quantify each group’s predictive value.

To assess age-prediction accuracy across the lifespan, we computed the mean absolute error (MAE) between predicted and chronological age within fixed-width age bins (5 years). MAEs were averaged within bins for each dataset, with 95% confidence intervals estimated via the Student’s t-distribution. To formally test for between-dataset differences in error, we applied Kruskal–Wallis tests within each age bin, followed by pairwise Mann–Whitney U tests. Multiple comparisons across bins and dataset pairs were controlled using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR), and we report FDR-adjusted q-values alongside raw p-values (**Supplementary Table 3**).

### **Cross-Species Validation**

To evaluate the generalizability of the PyHEARTS pipeline across species, we applied the same waveform modeling and feature extraction procedures to murine ECG recordings. These signals were obtained under light anesthesia from prior studies[53](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?B3dLe6), and were sampled at 3,000 Hz or higher to ensure adequate resolution of rapid deflections. This met the minimum requirement of 2,500 Hz for mouse ECG processing established by PyHEARTS.

Species-specific configuration settings were used to adapt to murine physiology, including narrower QRS complexes, higher heart rates, and lower-amplitude Q and S deflections. Aside from these parameter changes, the segmentation, detrending, Gaussian fitting, feature extraction, and quality control steps remained identical to those used for human data.

Beat-wise reconstructions and morphological features were successfully generated from mouse ECGs using the same unified processing framework. This cross-species application demonstrated that PyHEARTS can extract interpretable, physiologically relevant cardiac features from both human and mouse ECGs with minimal modification, supporting its use in translational research.

| PyHEARTS Output Variables Reference (per‑cycle CSV) |  |  |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| The table lists each column emitted by \*\_pyhearts.csv, with a plain‑language description and how it is computed in the toolbox. For all threshold and species-specific values, see Python object: ProcessCycleConfig. |  |  |
| **Feature Name** | **Description** | **Calculation** |
| **cycle\_index** | Cycle number (0-based) within the record | Index assigned during epoching; increments per retained R–R cycle |
| **cycle\_trend** | Estimated linear trend slope within the cycle | Slope from line through first and last samples after baseline subtraction (linergress) |
| **r\_squared** | Goodness-of-fit (R2) of Gaussian model | Squared Pearson correlation between detrended cycle and fitted sum of Gaussians |
| **rmse** | Root mean square error of fit | RMSE between detrended cycle and fitted waveform |
| **P\_global\_center\_idx** | P wave center (absolute sample index) | xs\_samples\[center\_idx\] after center refinement |
| **P\_global\_le\_idx** | P wave left edge (absolute sample index) | xs\_samples\[le\_idx\] where signal crosses fraction threshold (std-guided |
| **P\_global\_ri\_idx** | P wave right edge (absolute sample index) | xs\_samples\[ri\_idx\] where signal crosses fraction threshold (std-guided) |
| **P\_center\_ms** | P wave center time (ms) | (global\_center\_idx/fs)×1000 |
| **P\_le\_ms** | P wave left-edge time (ms) | (global\_le\_idx/fs)×1000 |
| **P\_ri\_ms** | P wave right-edge time (ms) | (global\_ri\_idx/fs)×1000 |
| **Q\_global\_center\_idx** | Q wave center (absolute sample index) | xs\_samples\[center\_idx\] after center refinement |
| **Q\_global\_le\_idx** | Q wave left edge (absolute sample index) | xs\_samples\[le\_idx\] where signal crosses fraction threshold (std-guided) |

| **R\_global\_le\_idx** | R peak left edge (absolute sample index) | xs\_samples\[le\_idx\] where signal crosses fraction threshold (std-guided) |

| **Heart Rate Variability Features** | **Description** | **Calculation** |
| **average\_heart\_rate** | Mean heart rate in beats per minute (bpm) | HRᵢ \= 60 ÷ (RRᵢ / 1000), where RRᵢ is the *i*\-th NN interval in milliseconds. The average heart rate is then: HR̄ \= (1/N) × Σ HRᵢ over all N beats |
| **sdnn** | Standard deviation of NN (normal-to-normal) intervals, in ms | Computed directly from the cleaned RR intervals: SDNN \= sqrt( (1 / (N − 1)) \* Σ from i=1 to N of (RR(i) − mean(RR))2 where mean(RR) is the average of the RR intervals. |
| **rmssd** | Root mean square of successive differences | Compute the successive differences: di \= RR(i+1) − RR(i). Then compute the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD): RMSSD \= sqrt( (1 / (N − 1)) \* Σ from i=1 to N−1 of (di2) ) |
| **nn50** | Number of successive RR differences greater than 50 ms | Count how many satisfy: NN50 \= Σ from i=1 to N−1 of 1(di \> 50 ms), where 1(condition) is an indicator function that equals 1 if the condition is true and 0 otherwise |

**Supplementary Table 4\. Species-specific configuration settings**

Two configuration presets, `for_human()` and `for_mouse()`, automatically apply these values. Users may override any field at runtime. The full resolved configuration, including all overrides and version tag (`v1-human` or `v1-mouse`), is saved with each output to ensure full reproducibility.

**![][image7]**

**Supplementary Figure 1\. PyHEARTS ECG fitting performance across diverse waveform morphologies.** 

Representative single-beat ECG segments (blue) and fitted P–QRS–T model (red) are shown for eight scenarios: normal PQRST, missing P wave, missing Q wave, missing S wave, missing T wave, inverted R wave, missing P and T waves, and QRS-only (no P or T). Vertical dashed lines mark the detected/fitted fiducial locations for P, Q, R, S and T components (labels at the corresponding markers), illustrating robust handling of absent components and polarity inversion while maintaining accurate localization of the QRS complex.

![][image8]

**Supplementary Figure 2\. Bland-Altman plots comparing PyHEARTS interval measurements against QTDB ground truth annotations.** 

Agreement between PyHEARTS and manual annotations for PR (n=2,603), QRS (n=7,441), QT (n=6,208), RT (n=2,725), and TT (n=3,143) intervals across 103 subjects. Each plot shows the difference (PyHEARTS − Ground Truth) versus the mean of the two methods, with mean bias (dashed red line) and 95% limits of agreement (dashed green lines, mean ± 1.96 SD). Data from the PhysioNet QT Database (QTDB).
